newsitem.title: USA: Defense in Oklahoma bomb trial attacks FBI lab.
newsitem.headline: Defense in Oklahoma bomb trial attacks FBI lab.

text.p: An FBI chemist testified on Tuesday that the lab used to analyse Oklahoma City bomb evidence was contaminated with explosives, a charge defence lawyers hope will undermine the case against Timothy McVeigh.

Frederic Whitehurst, an FBI agent and chemist whose complaints sparked an internal investigation into the crime lab, said he found the explosives residue contamination in May 1995, just weeks after the federal building was bombed killing 168 people.
Whitehurst said the explosives residue, found in four or five spots dotted around the lab, could jeopardise the reliability of the evidence.

"If we're processing evidence and we're contaminated ourselves then you don't know whether our finding of explosives material on a piece of evidence is a result of our contamination of the evidence ourselves or if the explosive residue was on the evidence before it got to us," he said.

However, under cross-examination by prosecutor Beth Wilkinson, Whitehurst admitted he had no proof the evidence had become contaminated. "I have no knowledge of any actual contamination of any evidence in this case," he testified.
Jurors watched intently as Whitehurst said other FBI agents who had handled and analysed explosives residue had not been officially qualified to do so.

Also paying close attention was McVeigh, who pleaded not guilty to the devastating attack. If found guilty, the Gulf War veteran faces the death penalty. His defence team is expected to wrap up its case this week.
Whitehurst was a star witness for the defence, which is fighting to dismantle a carefully constructed government case linking McVeigh to the April 19, 1995, Oklahoma City bombing.

He said he was baffled when FBI agent Steven Burmeister testified for the prosecution that crystals of ammonium nitrate were found embedded in a panel the government said came from the truck used in the bombing.

The panel, a crucial piece of evidence found near the bombing site, is believed to have been rained on before it was found, Whitehurst said -- exposure that normally would obliterate any ammonium nitrate traces.

"I don't know how that ammonium nitrate survived if it went through a rainstorm. I don't know how it could be on that evidence. It doesn't make sense to me," Whitehurst said. But while he said he was confused, he also testified that he was not claiming the crystals were placed there by anyone.

A British explosives expert testifying for the defence also criticised the FBI's procedures. John Lloyd said he had seen no evidence that testing for contaminants was conducted on McVeigh's clothes. Explosives traces were found on some of McVeigh's clothing, FBI agents have previously testified.

Whitehurst also testified he was told by FBI agent David Williams that the panel was found by a private citizen instead of trained investigators, which could call into question the "chain of custody" standard for ensuring that all evidence is guaranteed free of contamination.

Whitehurst quoted Williams as telling him: "We had a problem with the chain of custody and we're not going to use it." But Williams, who testified earlier on Tuesday, said he could not remember that conversation.

Whitehurst's testimony appeared damaging for the government, although he did admit under cross-examination he was not personally familiar with all the data on the ammonium nitrate, which the government said was the chief ingredient of the bomb.
He said he had formed his opinion based on the information available to him and admitted there could be factors involved about which he was not aware.
Nevertheless, his testimony dovetailed nicely with defence attempts to paint the FBI and government investigators as incompetent and overeager.

Williams, who had been criticised by name in a Justice Department report on the crime laboratory, testified earlier on Tuesday that there was no single person in charge of evidence collection at the scene, suggesting the evidence against McVeigh could be unreliable.
